summary: An excerpt from a novel (Book 11, part 6) in which a young girl explains how her family named its children after people in books or relatives, including Mira named after aunt Miranda, Mark after an uncle, and Jenny and Fanny after a singer and a dancer. The girl then talks with Mr. Cobb about her shoes, her schooling, her plans to become a painter like Miss Ross, and the difference between calling her farm Randall's Farm and Sunnybrook Farm. The passage ends with Rebecca's eyes unsettling Mr. Cobb. The note also contains an unrelated line about Yuki viewing a painting in 2013, which appears to be a stray insertion.
one_line: Excerpt from a novel where a girl explains her family's naming customs and argues with Mr. Cobb over calling her farm Sunnybrook Farm.
key_facts: Mira was named after aunt Miranda in Riverboro, in hopes it might do some good, but it did not, and the family now calls her Mira.
Hannah is named after Hannah at the Window Binding Shoes, and the narrator is taken out of Ivanhoe.
John Halifax was a gentleman in a book, and Mark is named after his uncle Marquis de Lafayette, who died a twin.
Jenny is named for a singer and Fanny for a beautiful dancer, but mother says they are both misfits.
Jenny cannot carry a tune and Fanny is kind of stiff-legged, according to the narrator's mother.
The narrator's mother says they must always stand up for father because everything was against him and he would not have died if he had not had such bad luck.
The narrator says the shoes she wears are spandy new and have to last six months.
In two years the narrator is going to the seminary at Wareham, which her mother says ought to be the making of her.
The narrator says she is going to be a painter like Miss Ross when she gets through school, though her mother thinks she had better teach.
The farm is called Randall's Farm by mother, but the narrator calls it Sunnybrook Farm.
Mr. Cobb says it does not make a difference what you call a farm so long as you know where it is.
The narrator says it does make a difference what you call things.
The note includes an unrelated line stating that in 2013, after waiting in line for hours, Yuki finally saw the original 'Garden of Earthly Delights' painting up close.
